It records his investigation of a harem conspiracy, his quarrying and canal work at the First Cataract, and five military campaigns against the 'Sand-Dwellers' of Sinai and southern Canaan, with an army drawn from Egypt, Nubia, and Libya.
Interpretations: Weni gives the earliest detailed Egyptian account of campaigning in the Sinai-Canaan region and shows Egypt already projecting power into the land later promised to Abraham centuries before the patriarchs. His 'Sand-Dwellers' are a general term for desert nomads, not Israelites, and the inscription says nothing about the patriarchs; it illuminates the world of the early second millennium BC, not a specific biblical event.
AlternativeNames: Inscription of Weni; Autobiography of Uni
BiblicalSignificance: It illuminates the Egyptian-Canaanite world of the third millennium BC in which the earliest biblical history is set, showing Egyptian armies already operating in Canaan long before Israel existed as a nation.

Description: A clay bulla barely a centimetre across, found in 1982 by Yigal Shiloh in the City of David, one of a hoard of 51 bullae from the 'house of bullae', reading 'Belonging to Azariah, son of Hilkiah'. Hilkiah was the high priest under King Josiah who found the Book of the Law in the Temple in 2 Kings 22:8, and the high-priestly genealogy names his son and successor Azariah (1 Chronicles 6:13-14; Ezra 7:1, where Azariah stands in Ezra's ancestry). The bulla dates to the late 7th century BC, roughly the time of Nebuchadnezzar's first siege of Jerusalem in 605 BC. Note: the bulla itself does not state Azariah's office; the identification with the high-priestly family rests on the two-generation name match, the date, and the stratified Jerusalem context.
Interpretations: This is a two-generation match to the Bible's high-priestly family, from a carefully controlled excavation, and it was found in the same hoard as the Gemariah son of Shaphan bulla, whose family served alongside Hilkiah's in Josiah's court. Together the two bullae corroborate the pairing of priest and scribe in 2 Kings 22. The identification is strong but not absolute, since the bulla does not give Azariah's title.
BiblicalSignificance: The seal of the high priest's son survives from the generation of Josiah's reform, corroborating the family behind the rediscovery of the Book of the Law.

Description: A fragmentary clay tablet from the reign of Sennacherib (705-681 BC), found in the mid-19th century in the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh and identified as a single tablet by Nadav Na'aman in 1974. Now in the British Museum (K.6205 + BM 82-3-23,131), it preserves part of Sennacherib's account of his 701 BC campaign against Hezekiah of Judah, describing Azekah as a stronghold on a mountain ridge, its walls rivaling the highest mountains, taken with siege ramps and battering rams, then spoiled, destroyed, and burned.
Interpretations: The inscription is independent Assyrian testimony to Sennacherib's 701 BC invasion of Judah, matching 2 Kings 18-19 and Isaiah 36-37, and it shows the campaign's devastation reaching Azekah, one of Judah's fortified cities. It is fragmentary: the surviving text does not mention Jerusalem or its deliverance, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the biblical account of Jerusalem's survival. It is distinct from the Taylor Prism (already on site as the Sennacherib Prism), which carries the fuller campaign narrative.
BiblicalSignificance: It corroborates Sennacherib's invasion of Judah and the fall of its fortified cities in 701 BC, the historical setting of Hezekiah's prayer and Jerusalem's deliverance.

Description: An archive of 35 legal papyri, dated AD 94-134, found in March 1961 by a team led by Yigael Yadin in a concealed hiding place in the Cave of Letters at Nahal Hever on the western shore of the Dead Sea. The papers were hidden in a leather satchel by Babatha, daughter of Shim'on, a Jewish woman of Maoza in Roman Arabia, who had fled to the cave with other Jewish refugees at the end of the Bar Kokhba revolt in AD 135. The archive contains marriage contracts, deeds of gift, court documents and records of date-palm orchards, including an orchard her father bought at Maoza in AD 99 and later gave to her.
Interpretations: Babatha's papers are the fullest surviving picture of an ordinary Jewish woman's legal life under Rome: she owned orchards, married twice, went to court, and kept every deed. The archive shows Jewish, Nabatean and Roman law operating side by side in one woman's affairs, and it gives the Bar Kokhba revolt a human scale, since these are the papers of people who hid and died rather than surrender them.
BiblicalSignificance: The archive illuminates daily Jewish life in Roman Arabia a generation after the New Testament, when the early church was spreading through exactly this world of deeds, courts and orchards.
DiscoveryLocation: Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever, Judean Desert

Description: Glazed-brick panels of striding lions that lined the Processional Way leading through the Ishtar Gate at Babylon, built under Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BC. About 120 lions marched along the walls of the sacred way, their mouths open, each panel made of moulded, polychrome-glazed bricks; some bricks are stamped with Nebuchadnezzar's name. Excavated by Robert Koldewey's German expedition between 1899 and 1917, the way was partly reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin, while individual panels went to museums including the Royal Ontario Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.
Interpretations: The lions are the art of the Babylon of Daniel's day: the lion was the symbol of Ishtar, goddess of love and war, and the panels lined the route of the annual New Year festival procession. They help readers picture the splendour of the city that carried Judah into exile, and they match the biblical picture of Babylon as a city of overwhelming display.
AlternativeNames: Striding Lions of Babylon;Ishtar Gate Lion Panels
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
BiblicalSignificance: The lions lined the ceremonial heart of the 'great Babylon' Nebuchadnezzar boasted of in Daniel 4:30, giving visible form to the city's pride that the book says God humbled.
CurrentLocation: Pergamon Museum, Berlin (reconstruction); Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto; Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; Istanbul Archaeology Museums (panels)
ImageCredit: Photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen (Public domain) — Ishtar Gate-type lion panel, not a Processional Way panel itself

Description: A silver sela (tetradrachm) of the Bar Kokhba revolt, about 25-27 mm and 13.6-14.4 g, struck AD 132-135. Like all Bar Kokhba coins, it was overstruck on a Roman provincial coin already in circulation (mainly tetradrachms and drachms of Antioch, Tyre, and Caesarea in Cappadocia, plus denarii), because the rebel government had no full mint of its own. The obverse shows the facade of the Jerusalem temple with a star above and 'Shim'on' (Simon) in Paleo-Hebrew, with the Ark of the Covenant or showbread table within; the reverse shows a lulav with an etrog and 'Year Two of the Freedom of Israel' or 'For the Freedom of Jerusalem'. Year 1 and 2 issues are dated; Year 3 (AD 134-135) issues are undated. This was the last Jewish coinage in antiquity.
Interpretations: The temple facade and star on the coin show that restoring the temple was a central goal of the revolt, and the name 'Shim'on' with the star is the visual form of the messianic title Bar Kokhba ('Son of the Star'). The rebels never captured Jerusalem - only 5 Bar Kokhba coins had been found in Jerusalem as of 2024 - so the temple on the coin is an aspiration, not a record of a rebuilt temple. The coin is a warning as well as a witness: it shows a messianic movement that ended in catastrophe.
AlternativeNames: Bar Kokhba Sela;Bar Kokhba Silver Shekel
BiblicalSignificance: Matthew 24:24 warns that false messiahs will appear and deceive many if possible; Bar Kokhba, hailed by many as messiah and pictured with a star on his coins, is presented here as an application of that warning, not as a direct identification of the verse.
CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem and other collections (examples)
DiscoveryLocation: Judaea (rebel-held areas; few found in Jerusalem)
ImageCredit: Photo: IsraelXKV8R (CC BY-SA 3.0) — Bar Kokhba zuz with trumpet and lyre, NOT a Temple-façade tetradrachm

Description: A large sacrificial altar of cut calcareous sandstone ashlars with chiselled horns on four corners, reconstructed to over 5 feet high (about 3 cubits, matching Exodus 27:1–2). Its stones were found in 1973 by Yohanan Aharoni at Tel Beersheba, reused in a storehouse wall in secondary use. The original is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem, and a reconstructed replica stands at the Tel Beersheba national park entrance. Burn marks show sacrifices were performed on it.
Interpretations: Two debates must be stated. First, when it was dismantled: Aharoni's 1973 press release linked the dismantling to Hezekiah's reform (2 Kings 18:1–4), while Yigael Yadin suggested it could be the altar of 2 Kings 23:8 destroyed by Josiah, and pottery from the dismantling layer has been dated 640–620 BCE, which points toward Josiah; most scholars now favour Hezekiah, but the question is not settled. Second, whom it served: its finely cut ashlars contrast with the unhewn stones of the Arad altar and with Deuteronomy 27:6's whole-stone rule, and one source suggests it may have served a pagan cult under kings such as Ahaz rather than Yahweh worship. Amos denounces worship at Beersheba (Amos 8:14).
BiblicalSignificance: It is the largest horned altar found in Israel and matches the tabernacle altar's dimensions in Exodus, while its deliberate dismantling illustrates the cultic reforms that centralised worship in Jerusalem.
CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (original); replica at Tel Beersheba

Description: A multilingual royal inscription and large rock relief carved high on a cliff at Mount Behistun, Kermanshah Province, Iran, established by the Achaemenid king Darius I (reigned 522–486 BC) around 520 BC. The text, about 1,200 lines in total across Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian versions, narrates Darius's accession and his defeat of the usurper Gaumata and nineteen rebel leaders within a single year. The monument, carved about 100 m up the cliff, was first copied by Henry Rawlinson between 1835 and 1847 and published in 1849; the work was a key to deciphering cuneiform. It remains in situ and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2006.
Interpretations: Behistun is the primary monument of Darius I, the king under whom temple work at Jerusalem resumed and was completed (Ezra 4:24; 5:1-17; 6:1-15). It illuminates the Persian administration and royal ideology of exactly the reign in which the returned exiles rebuilt. Caution: the inscription does not mention Judah or the temple — the connection is to Darius's reign, not to a biblical event directly. Also, Darius I of Ezra must not be conflated with 'Darius the Mede' of Daniel 6, a debated figure distinct from Darius I.
BiblicalSignificance: Behistun is the great self-portrait of Darius I, the Persian king whose decree let the returned exiles finish the temple (Ezra 6:1-15); it also gave scholars the key that unlocked cuneiform, opening the whole Assyrian and Babylonian record behind the Old Testament.
CurrentLocation: In situ, Mount Behistun, Iran (UNESCO World Heritage site)
ImageCredit: Drawing: Pascal Coste (Public domain) — 1840 drawing, not a photograph

Description: The mosaic floor of a synagogue at Beit Alpha in the Jezreel Valley, at the foot of Mount Gilboa, found in 1928 by kibbutzniks digging irrigation ditches and excavated by Eleazar Sukenik. Its three panels show the Binding of Isaac, a zodiac wheel with Helios driving a four-horse chariot at the centre, Hebrew zodiac names and the four seasons as female busts in the corners, and a Torah shrine panel naming the artists Marianos and his son Hanina. The synagogue is dated to the 5th-6th century AD, with sources differing between a 5th-century and a 6th-century date.
Interpretations: The mosaic shows a late-antique Jewish community decorating its synagogue with the zodiac and a sun-god figure, which raises the question of how such imagery sat alongside Jewish worship; scholars debate whether the zodiac was decorative, calendrical, or symbolic, and the mosaic must not be read as evidence about biblical-era worship, since it is half a millennium after the biblical period. The Binding of Isaac panel visualises Genesis 22 for a congregation that already knew the story.
AlternativeNames: Beit Alfa Synagogue Mosaic; Bet Alpha Synagogue Mosaic
BiblicalSignificance: The mosaic is a vivid visual retelling of the Binding of Isaac, showing how Genesis 22 stayed central to Jewish worship and art centuries after it was written.

Description: The Beni Hasan tomb paintings include the famous procession of the Aamu on the north wall of tomb BH3, belonging to the 12th-Dynasty official Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan, Egypt. Dated to year 6 of Senusret II, about 1892 BC, the scene shows West Asiatic visitors - 15 depicted, 37 named in the inscription - led by Absha (Abisha), called 'ruler of a foreign land' and described with the earliest known use of the title 'Hyksos,' bringing eye-paint and animals as offerings. The paintings were recorded by Lepsius in 1849 and published by Percy Newberry in 1893.
Interpretations: The painting is the classic visual evidence that West Asiatic (possibly Canaanite or Amorite) traders entered Egypt in the patriarchal era, dressed in colorful patterned garments and traveling with families, donkeys, and livestock - the same kind of movement Genesis describes for Abram and later Jacob's family. Caution is required: Abisha is not a biblical figure, the Aamu are not Israelites, and the scene is sometimes called Hyksos or 'forerunners' of the Hyksos only in a loose sense. It proves the plausibility and cultural setting of Genesis's Egypt journeys, not any specific biblical event.
AlternativeNames: Procession of the Aamu; Aamu Procession
BiblicalSignificance: Beni Hasan gives a face to the world of Genesis 12: Abram's journey into Egypt happened in an age when Asiatic caravans really did arrive at Egyptian officials' doors.
CurrentLocation: In situ, tomb BH3, Beni Hasan, Egypt
ImageCredit: Drawing: NebMaatRa (CC BY-SA 3.0) — drawing of the Aamu procession, not a photograph

Description: A granite pedestal-base fragment about 40 by 46 cm, from the Eighteenth or Nineteenth Dynasty, now in the Egyptian Museum of Berlin (AM 21687). It shows three bound prisoners with name rings reading Ashkelon, Canaan, and a broken third ring read by Manfred Gorg (2001) as 'Israel,' based on a vulture hieroglyph; later imaging and 3D work supported the vulture reading (van der Veen, Theis, Gorg 2010). The piece was purchased in 1913 from antiquities trader M. Nachman by Ludwig Borchardt and is unprovenanced.
HistoricalPeriod: New Kingdom, Eighteenth or Nineteenth Dynasty
Interpretations: If the third ring really reads 'Israel,' this would be an earlier extra-biblical mention of Israel than the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC). But the reading is rejected by scholars such as James Hoffmeier on linguistic grounds, the spelling would be unique, and the piece has no excavation context because it was bought on the antiquities market. It must be presented as a contested reading, not as the earliest mention of Israel.
BiblicalSignificance: It bears on the question of how early the name Israel appears outside the Bible, in the context of Egypt's campaigns among the peoples of Canaan; the reading itself remains disputed.
ArtifactDate: Eighteenth or Nineteenth Dynasty, c. 14th-13th century BC

Description: Bodmer Papyrus P66 (P. Bodmer II) is a nearly complete Greek codex of the Gospel of John, found in 1952 at Jabal Abu Mana near Dishna in Egypt. Its original editor dated it to about AD 200 on handwriting; Herbert Hunger argued for AD 100-150, while Brent Nongbri's broader study concluded the early or middle 4th century is more likely. The codex has 39 folios (156 pages), with the first 26 leaves almost fully intact. It is now housed at the Bibliotheca Bodmeriana in Cologny-Geneva, with one leaf in Cologne.
Interpretations: P66 is one of the oldest well-preserved New Testament manuscripts and a key witness to the Alexandrian text of John, very close to P75 and Codex Vaticanus. Like the other early papyri of John, it omits the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11), marking the omission with a dot and space, which demonstrates that the passage was absent from the earliest surviving copies of John. Its date range is genuinely disputed, so any single date should be given with its alternatives rather than stated as settled.
BiblicalSignificance: It is the oldest nearly complete Gospel of John, anchoring the text of John within about a century of its writing and confirming the early absence of the adulteress passage.
ArtifactDate: c. AD 200 (disputed: AD 100-150 to 4th century proposed)
CurrentLocation: Bodmer Library, Cologny-Geneva, Switzerland (one leaf in Cologne, Germany)

Description: Bodmer Papyrus P75 (P. Bodmer XIV-XV, now Hanna Papyrus 1) is an early Greek codex containing most of Luke and the beginning of John, found in the 1950s at Pabau in Egypt. Traditionally dated to about AD 175-225, though some recent studies argue for the late 3rd to early 4th century, it originally had about 144 pages, of which 102 survive. It was formerly in the Bodmer Library at Cologny and was presented to Pope Benedict XVI in 2007 by Frank Hanna; it is now in the Vatican Library, Rome.
Interpretations: P75 is often called the most significant New Testament papyrus discovered, because its text agrees with the 4th-century Codex Vaticanus almost exactly, vindicating the antiquity of the Vaticanus text-type a century before that codex was copied. It contains the oldest known copy of the Lord's Prayer in Luke and, like P66, omits the adulteress passage (John 7:53-8:11). Its combination of Luke and John in a single codex, with John beginning on the same page where Luke ends, shows the Gospels circulating together as a collection in early Egyptian Christianity.
BiblicalSignificance: Its near-identity with Codex Vaticanus proves the Vaticanus text of Luke and John already existed a century earlier, and it holds the oldest copy of Luke's Lord's Prayer.

Description: A papyrus from the Thirteenth Dynasty (early second millennium BC) listing 95 household servants, many specified as Asiatic or western Asian, now in the Brooklyn Museum. About 30 to 40 bear Semitic names, the servants of a noblewoman named Senebtisi, including forms resembling Shiphrah (the midwife of Exodus 1:15), Jacob, Job, and Issachar, alongside names such as Menahema and Ashera. The papyrus shows a household in Egypt staffed substantially by people from Canaan and Syria.
Interpretations: The papyrus is real evidence that Semitic-speaking servants from the Levant lived and worked in Egypt in the early second millennium BC, which fits the general setting of Israel's sojourn. But critics rightly warn against calling these names 'specifically Hebrew': they are Northwest Semitic names common across Semitic peoples, no distinct Hebrew language is identifiable this early, and one often-cited name (Hy'b'rw) is more likely 'Hay'abi-ilu' ('Where is my father, o El?'), not 'Hebrew.' It must never be presented as proof of Hebrew slaves in Egypt.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
BiblicalSignificance: It illuminates the world behind Exodus 1, in which people from Canaan lived as servants in Egyptian households, while stopping well short of proving the biblical account.

Description: The Bubastite Portal is the colonnaded forecourt and inscribed south wall of the Temple of Amun at Karnak, built by Shoshenq I (Sheshonq I), founder of Egypt's 22nd (Libyan or Bubastite) Dynasty, who reigned c. 943-923 BC. Its great relief, carved for his Levantine campaign of about 925 BC, shows the pharaoh smiting Asiatic enemies while the god Amun presents him with name-rings listing more than 150 towns and peoples conquered or subjugated in Israel and Judah, including Megiddo, Gezer, Arad, and Beth-Shean. Shoshenq is traditionally identified with the biblical Shishak, who marched against Jerusalem in the fifth year of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:25-28; 2 Chronicles 12:2-9).
HistoricalPeriod: Third Intermediate Period, 22nd Dynasty, c. 925 BC
Interpretations: The portal is the strongest Egyptian corroboration of a biblical king's campaign: an Egyptian king in the right decade lists conquests across exactly the Israelite and Judahite territory the Bible describes, and a Shoshenq victory-stele fragment was also found at Megiddo. The essential caution is that Jerusalem itself does not appear among the inscribed place names - scholars debate whether this reflects ideological selectivity, negotiated submission, or a campaign that differed from the biblical account, and a 2021 conference explicitly called for a fresh critical review. The portal therefore corroborates a Levantine campaign by the biblical Shishak's Egyptian counterpart; it does not by itself prove the Jerusalem sack or the temple treasures account.
AlternativeNames: Shishak Relief; Shishaq Relief; Shishak Inscription
BiblicalSignificance: The Bubastite Portal puts a named Egyptian king's own victory inscription beside the Bible's account of Shishak's invasion in Rehoboam's reign - the closest thing to an Egyptian royal record of a biblical campaign.

Description: Chester Beatty Papyrus P45 (P. Chester Beatty I) is a Greek codex containing portions of the four Gospels and Acts, dated to about AD 175-225. Found in Egypt, possibly in the Faiyum or at Aphroditopolis, it was purchased by Alfred Chester Beatty in 1931 and announced by Frederic Kenyon in 1933. Only 30 leaves survive of an original codex of about 220 pages. It is the earliest known example of the four Gospels gathered in one volume together with Acts.
Interpretations: P45 shows that by around AD 200, Christians were already collecting the four Gospels as a set, not circulating them only separately. Its text is eclectic with an Alexandrian leaning, classed Category I, and its shorter readings in places illustrate how later scribes sometimes expanded the text. One leaf (Matthew 25:41-26:39) is in Vienna rather than Dublin, a reminder that ancient codices were often split by the antiquities trade.
ScriptureIlluminated: Matthew 20-21; Matthew 25-26; Mark 4-9; Mark 11-12; Luke 6-7; Luke 9-14; John 4-5; John 10-11; Acts 4-17
BiblicalSignificance: It is the earliest codex gathering all four Gospels with Acts, showing the fourfold Gospel collection already existed around AD 200.
CurrentLocation: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin (one leaf at the Austrian National Library, Vienna)

Description: Chester Beatty Papyrus P46 (P. Chester Beatty II) is a Greek codex of Paul's letters, dated to about AD 175-225 and most often placed around AD 200. Found in Egypt, most likely in the Faiyum, it was purchased in 1930-31 and published in the 1930s. Of about 104 leaves, 86 survive: 56 in Dublin and 30 at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. It contains Romans (from 5:17), Hebrews, 1-2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Galatians, Philippians, Colossians, and 1 Thessalonians, in that order.
Interpretations: P46 is the earliest extensive witness to a collected Paul, and its order is itself evidence: Hebrews placed directly after Romans shows that Egyptian Christians by about AD 200 already counted Hebrews among Paul's letters. Its Alexandrian text, closest to Codex Vaticanus, anchors many readings of the Pauline epistles a century before the great parchment codices. The Romans doxology (16:25-27) appears after chapter 15, illustrating that even the arrangement of Romans was not yet fixed. A late-1st-century date proposed in 1988 has gained little acceptance, and some scholars prefer a 3rd-century date, so its dating should be stated as a range.
RelatedBooks: Romans; Hebrews; 1 Corinthians; 2 Corinthians; Ephesians; Galatians; Philippians; Colossians; 1 Thessalonians
ScriptureIlluminated: Romans 5:17-16:27; Hebrews 1:1-13:25; 1 Corinthians 1:1-16:24; 2 Corinthians 1:1-13:13; Ephesians 1:1-6:24; Galatians 1:1-6:18; Philippians 1:1-4:23; Colossians 1:1-4:18; 1 Thessalonians 1:1-5:28
BiblicalSignificance: It is the earliest large collection of Paul's letters, proving the Pauline corpus circulated as a set by about AD 200, with Hebrews already included.
CurrentLocation: Chester Beatty Library, Dublin; University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

Description: The rule book for the life and organization of the yahad, the communal group at Qumran, and one of the original seven scrolls from Cave 1, found in 1946–1947. The most complete copy, 1QS, is dated paleographically to about 100–75 BC, with ten further copies from Cave 4 (4Q255–264a) and one from Cave 5 (5Q11). It covers admission, shared property, prayer, meals, study and rigorous purity, and includes the 'Treatise on the Two Spirits' (1QS iii.13–iv.26), a penal code, a covenant-renewal liturgy, and expectation of the Prophet and the Messiahs of Aaron and Israel.
Interpretations: The Community Rule is the primary source for the sect's dualism (Spirit of Light versus Spirit of Darkness), predestination and communal discipline, and it shows a Judaism organized as a separated, priestly community awaiting the end. Authorship by the Teacher of Righteousness is hypothesized but unproven, and the Rule describes the sect's own ideals, not mainstream Jewish practice.
AlternativeNames: Manual of Discipline;Serekh ha-Yahad;Rule of the Community
BiblicalSignificance: It gives the clearest window into a disciplined Second Temple community's daily life and theology, and its 'prepare the way' self-understanding parallels the ministry of John the Baptist.
CurrentLocation: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem

Description: The only Dead Sea Scroll written on metal: three copper sheets (about 99% copper with about 1% tin) riveted end to end, about 2.4 metres by 28 centimetres, with letters punched into the metal in a Hebrew dialect close to Mishnaic Hebrew. It was found on 14 March 1952 at the back of Qumran Cave 3 by Henri de Contenson's team, in two oxidized rolls, and was cut into 23 strips at Manchester in 1955–56 because corrosion made unrolling impossible. It is not a religious text but a list of about 64 treasure caches — gold, silver and vessels — each with place, direction and depth directions, and it is now at the Jordan Museum, Amman.
Interpretations: The Copper Scroll illuminates the world of hidden wealth, revolt and temple treasure in first-century Judea, and it is dated by many scholars to the First Jewish Revolt period (about 66–70 AD). Whether its treasure was real Temple treasure, the community's own wealth, or a legendary list is unresolved, and no cache has ever been conclusively identified from its directions, so it must not be treated as a working treasure map.
BiblicalSignificance: It is a unique material witness to the turmoil of first-century Judea, when temple wealth and hiding valuables from Rome were urgent realities behind the world of the New Testament.
ArtifactDate: c. 50–100 AD (many scholars: First Jewish Revolt period, c. 66–70 AD)
ImageCredit: Photo: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Description: A rule text of the Qumran-associated community, first published by Solomon Schechter from two medieval manuscripts (10th and 12th centuries AD) found in 1896–1897 in the Cairo Geniza of the Ben Ezra Synagogue. Ten further copies were later found at Qumran (4Q266–273, 5Q12, 6Q15); the oldest Qumran copies date to the late 2nd–early 1st centuries BC, and the work was likely composed or redacted in the mid-2nd century BC. It has two parts: an exhortation recalling the community's origins and a body of statutes on marriage, purity, oaths, Sabbath, food and communal organization, and it introduces the Teacher of Righteousness and the Wicked Priest.
Interpretations: The Document is the fullest picture of the sect's self-understanding: a covenant community that saw itself as the faithful remnant after separating from a corrupt establishment. Whether its 'Damascus' is literal Syria, symbolic exile, or Qumran itself is debated (it quotes Amos 5:27 on exile 'beyond Damascus'), so the place name must not be read as a simple travel record. Its identification of the group with the Essenes is common but debated.
AlternativeNames: Zadokite Fragments;Document of the New Covenant in the Land of Damascus;CD
BiblicalSignificance: It shows a Second Temple Jewish community organizing its whole life around covenant obedience and purity, the world from which both Rabbinic Judaism and the early church emerged.
ArtifactDate: Mid-2nd century BC (composition); oldest Qumran copies late 2nd–early 1st century BC
CurrentLocation: Cambridge University Library (Cairo Geniza copies); Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Qumran fragments)
DiscoveryLocation: Cairo Geniza, Ben Ezra Synagogue; Qumran caves

Description: 4Q41, the All Souls Deuteronomy, is a Hebrew manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, found in 1952 and dated to the early Herodian period (30-1 BC). Two small sheets of exceptionally well-preserved parchment survive, containing Deuteronomy 5:1-6:1, including the full Ten Commandments, and Deuteronomy 8:5-10. It is the oldest surviving copy of the Decalogue. Its script is unusually tiny, with the letters waw and yod nearly indistinguishable.
Interpretations: The scroll's Decalogue harmonizes toward the Exodus version, uniquely adding the Exodus reason for the Sabbath commandment, showing that the two versions of the commandments influenced each other in transmission. Its unusual ordering suggests it was an excerpt collection for liturgical or devotional use rather than a complete scroll of Deuteronomy, though John Strugnell suggested it may have been repaired incorrectly. Its fuller spelling than the Masoretic Text and Samaritan Pentateuch illustrates the variety of Hebrew spelling in the Second Temple period.
AlternativeNames: 4QDeut-n; All Souls Deuteronomy; Ten Commandments Scroll
BiblicalSignificance: It is the oldest surviving copy of the Ten Commandments, written a century before Christ, and shows the Decalogue already circulating as a devotional text.

Description: 4Q2, also called 4QGen-b, is a Hebrew manuscript of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, found in 1952. Written in a Roman-period hand (1st century AD), it survives only in fragments containing Genesis 1:1-27; 2:14-19; 4:2-4; and 5:13. Though small, it is one of many Genesis copies at Qumran showing the book's early circulation.
Interpretations: Its fragments cover the creation account, the garden, Cain and Abel, and the genealogy of Adam, giving a first-century witness to the opening chapters of Genesis. The readings align broadly with the Masoretic tradition, adding to the evidence that Genesis was transmitted stably. Its fragmentary state is a caution: it illuminates only the verses it preserves.
BiblicalSignificance: It is a first-century witness to the opening chapters of Genesis, confirming that the creation and early genealogies were already fixed in essentially their present form.

Description: 4Q71, also called 4QJer-b, is a Hebrew manuscript of Jeremiah from Qumran Cave 4, found in 1952 and dated to the early 2nd century BC (about 200 BC). Only about 10 percent survives, with fragments of Jeremiah 9:22-10:21, including just 31 legible words in the key fragment. It is one of the oldest surviving copies of Jeremiah.
Interpretations: The scroll agrees with the shorter Greek Septuagint edition of Jeremiah against the longer Masoretic Text in verse order and brevity, supporting the view that the Septuagint translated an earlier, shorter Hebrew edition of Jeremiah rather than abbreviating a longer one. This matters for Bible study because Jeremiah exists in two genuinely different ancient editions, and neither can simply be assumed to be the 'original' throughout. Its fragmentary state means it illuminates only the verses it preserves.
BiblicalSignificance: It confirms that the shorter Septuagint form of Jeremiah rests on a real, earlier Hebrew edition, not on a translator's cuts.

Description: 4Q51, also called 4QSama, is the most extensive Samuel manuscript from Qumran, written in Hebrew in the Herodian period (about 50-25 BC). Hundreds of fragments survive from what was originally a scroll of some 55-60 columns, spanning 1 Samuel 1 through 2 Samuel 24. It was found in Qumran Cave 4 in 1952. Its readings often agree with the ancient Greek Septuagint against the later Masoretic Text.
Interpretations: The scroll's most famous contribution is a longer passage before 1 Samuel 11:1 describing Nahash's oppression of the Gadites and Reubenites, gouging out their right eyes, with 7,000 escaping to Jabesh-Gilead; this explains the sudden opening of chapter 11 and was adopted by modern translations such as the NRSV. Whether that passage is original or a secondary expansion is debated: Frank Moore Cross and Emanuel Tov accept it as original, while Dominique Barthelemy and others view it as an expansion, a stalemate noted in recent scholarship. Either way, the scroll shows that more than one Hebrew form of Samuel circulated in the Second Temple period.
BiblicalSignificance: It supplies the missing background to 1 Samuel 11 and proves that the Hebrew text of Samuel existed in more than one ancient form, sometimes agreeing with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text.

Description: The Egyptian execration texts are ritual curse texts inscribed on pottery sherds and figurines of bound prisoners, which were then smashed and buried to magically neutralize Egypt's enemies. The earliest examples come from the Old Kingdom, but the famous groups are the Berlin texts (pottery sherds naming about 20 Canaanite and Phoenician places and over 30 rulers, published by Kurt Sethe in 1926) and the Brussels texts (figurines from Saqqara naming 64 places, published by Georges Posener in 1957), with a further Mirgissa group published by Yvan Koenig in 1990. The Berlin texts date to the end of the 11th into the 12th Dynasty, early in the second millennium BC.
Interpretations: The execration texts are a gold mine for the geography of Canaan around 1900-1800 BC: they name Shechem, Ashkelon, Hazor, and other Canaanite towns, and the Berlin texts contain possibly the first known mention of Jerusalem (read as Rushalimum) - but that reading is debated, so Jerusalem's attestation here must be called 'possible,' not certain. The texts also warn against over-reading: they list enemies real and conventional, and their purpose was magic, not history-writing, so each name must be weighed rather than taken as a census of Canaan.
AlternativeNames: Berlin Texts; Brussels Texts; Mirgissa Texts
BiblicalSignificance: The execration texts independently confirm that the Canaanite towns of the Bible were real, named places in Egypt's world a thousand years before Israel's monarchy - and may preserve the earliest mention of Jerusalem anywhere.
CurrentLocation: Egyptian Museum, Berlin; Royal Museums of Art and History, Brussels
DiscoveryLocation: Saqqara; Thebes; Mirgissa, Nubia; and other Egyptian sites

Description: A small basalt fragment (12.5 cm high x 14 cm wide) inscribed in Moabite, dated about 840 BC (KAI 306), acquired by the Jordan Archaeological Museum in 1958 after reportedly being found at Kerak. Three incomplete lines survive, naming 'K]moshyat, king of Moab, the D[ibonite,' in the temple of Chemosh, on what was originally part of a statue or relief (belt, pleated skirt, and navel visible). It is distinct from the Mesha Stele and must not be merged with it.
Interpretations: The inscription is read by some scholars as commissioned by King Chemoshyat, father of Mesha, or by Mesha himself, a proposed reading of the broken first line as 'I am Mesha, son of Kemoshyat,' placing it in the world of Mesha's rebellion against Israel in 2 Kings 3. Cautions: the text is fragmentary, accounts of the finder differ, and the Mesha reading is a proposal, not established; a distinctive four-stroke He letter (versus the usual three strokes) is a noted paleographic feature.
BiblicalSignificance: It adds a second Moabite royal inscription from the age of Mesha's rebellion, confirming Moabite kingship and the Chemosh cult in the same period as 2 Kings 3.

Description: An Aramaic letter from Hananiah to Yedaniah and the Jewish garrison at Elephantine, Egypt, dated to year 5 of King Darius II (419 BC) and catalogued as Cowley 21 (Sachau 6). It instructs the garrison to count fourteen days of Nisan, observe Passover on the 14th at twilight, and keep the Festival of Unleavened Bread from the 15th to the 21st of Nisan, with no leaven seen or eaten from the 14th at sunset to the 21st, no work on the 15th and 21st, and ritual purity; it was sent by order of King Darius via Arsames, satrap of Egypt. The surviving fragment measures about 11.4 x 23 cm and was found in 1907 during German excavations at Elephantine; it is now in the Egyptian Museum of Berlin.
Interpretations: The earliest extra-biblical evidence for Passover observance: it shows a diaspora Jewish military community in Egypt keeping Passover and Unleavened Bread under a Persian royal order relayed through the satrap, and keeping the two festivals as distinct observances at that date. Cautions: the papyrus is fragmentary, and the word 'Pesach' itself is reconstructed in a lacuna (translations bracket it) — the identification rests on the unleavened-bread instructions. The suggestion that Hananiah was the brother of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 1:2; 7:2) is speculation, not established. The letter illuminates Passover observance; it does not prove the Exodus event itself.
BiblicalSignificance: The letter's rules mirror the Passover and Unleavened Bread instructions of Exodus 12, showing those festivals observed by a Jewish community in Egypt centuries after the Exodus account's setting.

Description: Two identical seal impressions (bullae) unearthed in 2014 in renewed excavations at Tel Lachish led by Yosef Garfinkel, Michael Hasel and Martin Klingbeil, reported in the Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research in May 2019. The first was found in situ inside a small juglet in the destruction layer left by Sennacherib's assault on Lachish (Lachish level III, 701 BC); the second was identified months later after the surrounding earth was wet-sifted in Jerusalem. The inscription reads 'Belonging to Eliakim (son of) Yehozarah'. Scholars propose the impressions may belong to Eliakim son of Hilkiah, chief steward of King Hezekiah, who held the key of the house of David (Isaiah 22:20-22) and negotiated with Sennacherib's officials (2 Kings 18:18). These are not the 'Eliakim, steward of Yaukin' jar-handle impressions from Tell Beit Mirsim and Beth Shemesh, which were once linked to King Jehoiachin but are now dated to the late 8th century BC.
Interpretations: The impressions come from exactly the right context for Hezekiah's steward, the 701 BC destruction of Lachish, but the patronymic on the seal is Yehozarah, not Hilkiah, so the identification with the biblical Eliakim is proposed, not certain, and the entry is classed Contextual for that reason. The case is still suggestive: a senior official's seal, sealed in the destruction debris of the Assyrian campaign the Bible describes.
BiblicalSignificance: Seals from the ashes of Sennacherib's destruction of Lachish may bear the name of Hezekiah's chief steward, the man Isaiah says held the key of David's house.
ArtifactDate: Late 8th century BC (701 BC destruction layer)

Description: The Babylonian creation epic, named from its opening words 'When on high,' about a thousand lines on seven cuneiform tablets in Old Babylonian, recited each year on the fourth day of the Akitu (New Year) festival. Recovered by Austen Henry Layard in 1849 in fragmentary form in the ruined Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh and published by George Smith in 1876, it tells how the gods Apsu (fresh water) and Tiamat (salt water) gave birth to the gods, how Marduk defeated Tiamat and split her body to form heaven and earth, and how humankind was created from a slain god's blood to serve the gods. Most of Tablet V has never been recovered.
Interpretations: Enuma Elish is a PARALLEL to Genesis 1, not proof of it and not its source in any simple sense: both begin with watery chaos, a dividing of waters, and a divine rest after creation, and both have the gods consulting before making man ('Let us make man,' Genesis 1:26). But the differences are decisive: Genesis has one God creating by word alone, without battle, without gods, and with humanity made in God's image for dominion, not as slaves to feed the gods. The epic's real value is showing what Israel's neighbors believed, which throws Genesis' distinctiveness into relief. Claims that Genesis was 'based on' the Babylonian myth overstate the evidence.
AlternativeNames: Epic of Creation; Seven Tablets of Creation
BiblicalSignificance: It is the great Babylonian creation story against which Genesis 1 must be read: the contrasts (one God, creation by word, humanity in God's image) are as instructive as the shared imagery of waters and divine rest.
ArtifactDate: Composed c. 18th-16th century BC (some scholars c. 1100 BC); Nineveh copies 7th century BC

Description: Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh is the famous 'Flood Tablet,' in which the hero Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how the gods sent a flood, how the god Ea warned him to build a boat, load it with animals, and survive, and how he released birds to find dry land and offered sacrifice afterward. The best-known copy (British Museum K.3375) comes from the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh and dates to the 7th century BC, though versions of the story are at least a thousand years older. Excavated at Kouyunjik by Austen Henry Layard (1849) and Hormuzd Rassam (1853), it was identified and translated by George Smith in December 1872.
Interpretations: The Flood Tablet is the best-known Mesopotamian parallel to Noah's flood, sharing the divine warning, the boat, the animals, the landing, the birds, and the sacrifice - but it is a parallel, not proof of the Genesis account. Its gods flood the world for secret, inscrutable reasons and then squabble over the survivor, while Genesis gives a moral cause (human wickedness) and a covenant. The tablet's fame also matters historically: its 1872 translation stunned Victorian readers by showing a flood story older than the previously known texts.
BiblicalSignificance: Tablet XI confirms that a flood story with Noah-like details circulated in Mesopotamia long before and alongside Israel, sharpening the question of what Genesis uniquely claims about God and judgment.

Description: The Eridu Genesis is a fragmentary Sumerian creation-and-flood tablet (CBS 10673) excavated at Nippur by the University of Pennsylvania expedition in 1893, first recognized as a creation-flood narrative by Arno Poebel in 1912 and published in 1914. Reconstructed and named by Thorkild Jacobsen in 1981, it dates to about 1600 BC. It tells how the gods created the 'black-headed people,' kingship descended from heaven, the first cities were founded (Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar, Shuruppak), the gods decreed a flood, and Ziusudra survived in a boat, sacrificed, and was granted eternal life in Dilmun.
Interpretations: The Eridu Genesis is the oldest surviving Mesopotamian flood composition in this tradition, and its creation-cities-flood sequence parallels Genesis 1-11 - but it is badly damaged, with large gaps reconstructed from context, and it is a parallel, not proof of the biblical account. Its gods create people as laborers, decree the flood in assembly, and reward the survivor with immortality, while Genesis presents one Creator, a flood as judgment on wickedness, and Noah as the head of a new humanity under covenant.
AlternativeNames: Sumerian Creation Myth; Sumerian Flood Story
BiblicalSignificance: As the earliest Mesopotamian creation-flood text, the Eridu Genesis shows how ancient the creation-flood storyline is, and throws Genesis's distinctive claims about one God and human purpose into relief.

Description: A six-sided clay prism, 33 cm tall, inscribed with 493 lines of cuneiform, dated to 673–672 BCE. It was found in the 1927–28 excavation season at Nineveh by Reginald Campbell Thompson and records Esarhaddon's reign and building projects. Among the kings supplying materials for his palace at Nineveh it names 'Menasii, king of Judah' — Manasseh. The prism was published by Thompson in 1931 by order of the trustees of the British Museum, where it is held.
Interpretations: The prism names Manasseh of Judah as a tributary king supplying building materials, confirming Manasseh as a historical vassal of Assyria during the period 2 Kings 21 and 2 Chronicles 33 describe. It does not mention his reported capture and repentance (2 Chronicles 33:11-13), which comes from the biblical account alone. Caution: several Esarhaddon prisms exist with parallel texts — this entry is specifically the prism from Thompson's 1927–28 Nineveh excavations; parallel texts are a naming caution, not an authenticity dispute.
BiblicalSignificance: By naming 'Manasseh, king of Judah' among Assyria's tributaries, the prism confirms the historical existence and vassal status of the king whose long reign 2 Kings 21 and 2 Chronicles 33 describe.

Description: A loyalty oath imposed by Esarhaddon in 672 BC on vassals across the empire - including, scholars argue, Judah under King Manasseh - to secure the succession of his son Ashurbanipal after the murder of Sennacherib by his own sons. The text, several hundred lines on a tablet about 40 by 28 centimeters, binds each oath-taker to protect Ashurbanipal, report any conspiracy, and accept elaborate curses for disloyalty, sworn before the gods as witnesses. The best-known copies were found in 1955 in the throne room of the Nabu temple at Nimrud (Kalhu); a further copy found at Tell Tayinat in 2009 showed the oath was administered in provincial ceremonies across the empire, not only at court.
Interpretations: The treaty is the closest ancient parallel to Deuteronomy's covenant form - preamble, divine witnesses, stipulations, curses, public reading, and a no-alteration clause - and many scholars think it shaped how Deuteronomy was written or heard in Manasseh's Judah. That influence is debated: it is a form parallel, not proof of copying, and the treaty must not be presented as the source of Deuteronomy. Judah's inclusion is inferred from Manasseh's vassal status and the empire-wide administration of the oath, not from a surviving Judah copy.
BiblicalSignificance: It illuminates the covenant world of Deuteronomy and the political pressure on Manasseh's Judah, where loyalty to Assyria and loyalty to the LORD pulled in opposite directions.
CurrentLocation: British Museum, London, and Iraq Museum, Baghdad (Nimrud copies); Turkey (Tell Tayinat copy)
DiscoveryLocation: Nimrud, Iraq (Nabu temple throne room); Tell Tayinat, Turkey (temple Building XVI)

FindName: Esarhaddon's Treaty with Ba'al of Tyre
Description: A vassal treaty imposed by the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (680-669 BC) on Ba'al I, king of Tyre, dated by its eponym year to the mid-670s BC. The text binds Ba'al to loyalty to the crown prince Ashurbanipal after Esarhaddon's death, requires him to report conspiracies against the crown, and seals the oath with curses on anyone who breaks it. It is one of a series of loyalty oaths Esarhaddon imposed on vassals across the empire, and it survives in a badly preserved text.
Interpretations: The treaty's chief value for Bible study is its form: preamble, stipulations, witnesses, curses, and public reading closely parallel the covenant structure of Deuteronomy, illuminating what a biblical covenant would have sounded like to its first hearers. That is a form parallel, not evidence that Deuteronomy copies this treaty. The treaty also confirms Tyre as an Assyrian vassal in the 7th century BC, the political background of the Tyre oracles in Isaiah 23 and Ezekiel 26-28. Note the text is badly preserved, so detailed stipulations should be quoted with caution.
BiblicalSignificance: It shows the treaty-covenant world in which Deuteronomy's blessings and curses were written, and it confirms Tyre's vassal status under Assyria in the generation before its judgment oracles.

Description: An inscription incised before firing on the shoulder of a large ceramic storage jar, reading 'Eshba'al son of Beda' (also written Ishba'al) in Canaanite script. Sherds of the jar were excavated at Khirbet Qeiyafa in the Valley of Elah in 2012 and restored by the excavation team, and the inscription was deciphered by Yosef Garfinkel, Saar Ganor, Mitka Golub and Haggai Misgav. The jar dates to the late 11th to early 10th century BCE, and it is the first time the name Eshbaal has appeared in an ancient inscription.
Interpretations: The reading itself is large, clear and written by a skilled hand, so the inscription's text is not in doubt. What is debated is how much weight it carries: this Eshbaal is NOT Saul's son, because his father is Beda, a name unique to this inscription and absent from the Bible. Scholars note the chronological pattern instead: the name Eshbaal appears in the Bible and now in archaeology only during David's reign, in the first half of the 10th century BCE, and was not used later in the First Temple period. The Bible itself preserves the name two ways: 1 Chronicles 8:33 keeps Eshbaal, while 2 Samuel 2:10 renders the same Saulide as Ish-bosheth ('man of shame'), reflecting reluctance over the Baal theophoric element.
BiblicalSignificance: It shows a Baal-theophoric Israelite name in everyday use in David's generation, exactly the period in which the Bible places the name Eshbaal, and it illustrates why the biblical writers sometimes replaced such names.

Description: An Egyptian-made amphibolite sarcophagus (2.56 x 1.25 m) of Eshmunazar II, Phoenician king of Sidon (reigned about 539-525 BC, son of Tabnit), discovered in January 1855 at the Magharat Abloun (Cavern of Apollo) necropolis near Sidon. Its 22-line Phoenician inscription (KAI 14) is the first Phoenician-language inscription discovered in Phoenicia proper and the most detailed found up to that point. It is now in the Louvre (AO 4806).
Interpretations: The inscription, in a Canaanite dialect mutually intelligible with Biblical Hebrew, records that the 'Lord of Kings' (the Persian king) granted the Sidonian kings Dor, Joppa, and the Plain of Sharon, coastal cities that appear in Joshua and Jonah. The sarcophagus was likely carved in Egypt from Wadi Hammamat stone and possibly captured as booty in Cambyses II's 525 BC conquest of Egypt. Sources differ on the discovery day (19 vs 20 January 1855), so only 'January 1855' is given.
AlternativeNames: Sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II; Eshmunazor Sarcophagus
BiblicalSignificance: It documents Persian-period Phoenician control of Dor and Joppa, two coastal cities named in Joshua and Jonah, in a language closely akin to Biblical Hebrew.
DiscoveryLocation: Magharat Abloun necropolis, near Sidon, Lebanon

FindName: First Jewish Revolt Year Five Silver Shekel
Description: A silver shekel of the First Jewish Revolt, about 13.25-13.9 g, dated Year 5 (April to August AD 70), with the same chalice and 'Shekel of Israel' obverse and pomegranates and 'Jerusalem the Holy' reverse as the earlier years. Year 5 shekels are the rarest of all First Revolt shekels - about 12 to 13 known from the classic die sets according to the Menorah Coin Project - struck in only about four months before Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed the temple in the autumn of AD 70. Several Year 5 shekels were excavated at Masada, showing that some fighters escaped Jerusalem before it fell.
Interpretations: Meshorer noted the striking fact that silver shekels kept being minted in the last four months of the war even after bronze coinage stopped entirely, because paying the half-shekel temple tax remained all-important to the defenders. After the war the revolt coins were banned and many were melted for their silver, which helps explain their rarity. The Year 5 shekel is therefore evidence of worship continuing under siege, not of a functioning economy.
BiblicalSignificance: Exodus 30:13 is the tax these last shekels were struck to pay, and Matthew 24:2 records Jesus's prediction that not one stone of the temple would be left on another - the destruction that ended their minting within months.
CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem and other collections (examples)

FindName: First Jewish Revolt Year Two Silver Shekel
Description: A silver shekel of the First Jewish Revolt, about 13.7-14 g, struck at Jerusalem and dated Year 2 (April AD 67 to March AD 68). The obverse shows a ritual chalice (omer cup) with a pearled rim and the Paleo-Hebrew legend 'Shekel of Israel' with 'Year Two' above; the reverse shows a staff with three pomegranate buds and 'Jerusalem the Holy'. These were the first coins struck by a sovereign Jewish government in silver, probably minted within the temple complex from temple stocks of Tyrian shekels. A Year 2 example found in Jerusalem's City of David was announced by the Israel Antiquities Authority in 2021.
Interpretations: The Year 2 shekel is a declaration of independence in silver: a Jewish government replacing the Tyrian shekel for the temple tax with its own coinage, dated by the years of the revolt rather than by any emperor. Year 2 shekels are relatively common (the Menorah Coin Project counts 360 or more known), which shows the revolt's mint working at scale in its second year.
BiblicalSignificance: Exodus 30:13 institutes the half-shekel temple tax; the revolt shekels were struck so that tax could still be paid in Jewish silver after the break with Rome, showing temple worship continuing even in wartime.
CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem and other collections (examples)

Description: An eschatological midrash from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script, that strings together biblical quotations with commentary: 2 Samuel 7:10–14, Exodus 15:17–18, Amos 9:11, Psalm 1:1, Psalm 2:1, Daniel 12:10 and others. Following Annette Steudel, it is now usually read as part of a larger eschatological midrash rather than a standalone anthology. It presents the sectarian doctrine identifying the Community with the Temple and announces two coming figures: the 'Branch of David' and the 'Interpreter of the Law', who will arise together in Zion in the last days.
Interpretations: The Florilegium is the clearest example of the sect's thematic interpretation: scattered promises are gathered to prove that the community itself is the true temple and that a Davidic messiah and a priestly interpreter will come together. Its exegesis is the sect's own reading, not the plain sense of the quoted passages, and its 'Branch of David' is the sect's royal messiah, not a named historical king.
AlternativeNames: Midrash on the Last Days;4Q Eschatological Commentary A
BiblicalSignificance: It shows how Second Temple Jews read the prophets messianically, gathering Davidic and priestly promises into one end-times hope — the same two-messiah expectation behind the Community Rule.
ArtifactDate: Herodian period (1st century BC–1st century AD)

Description: Glazed siliceous-brick panels from the palace of Darius I at Susa, made about 510 BC in the Achaemenid Persian period, excavated by Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy in 1885-1886 and now largely in the Louvre. Reconstructed into a procession of life-sized elite guards - the 'Immortals' - each figure about 17 bricks high, the frieze shows archers in patterned robes carrying spear, bow, and quiver. Though included in this Assyrian batch, it is Persian, not Assyrian: it belongs to the empire that succeeded Assyria and ruled Judah's world after the exile.
Interpretations: The frieze shows the splendor of the Persian court at Susa, the very palace where the book of Esther is set and where Nehemiah served as cupbearer. Its guards in procession are the visible power of the empire that let the exiles return and rebuild. It is Achaemenid art of Darius I's reign, a generation before Esther's Ahasuerus (Xerxes), so it sets the scene for Esther rather than illustrating its events.
AlternativeNames: Archers' Frieze; Frieze of the Immortals
BiblicalSignificance: It gives a face to the Persian court at Susa - the palace, the guards, the splendor - in which Esther, Mordecai, and Nehemiah lived and acted.
CurrentLocation: Louvre, Paris (some panels on loan elsewhere, including the British Museum)
DiscoveryLocation: Susa, Iran (Apadana, palace of Darius I)
ImageCredit: Photo: Jastrow (Public domain) — Darius I palace frieze, Louvre AOD 487, not an Assyrian frieze

Description: A clay bulla found in 2008 by Eilat Mazar in the City of David (Area G), in the same strata and a few yards from the Jehucal bulla, reading 'Gedaliah son of Pashhur'. Gedaliah son of Pashhur is named in Jeremiah 38:1 among the princes who sought Jeremiah's death for preaching surrender to Babylon, and his family is tied to Jeremiah 20, where Pashhur son of Immer, chief officer of the Temple, had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks.
Interpretations: Like the Jehucal bulla found beside it, this is a direct match to Jeremiah 38: the seal of a named opponent of Jeremiah, from the same Jerusalem strata and the same final generation of Judah. The pair of bullae together corroborate the court's cast of characters in Jeremiah's last years.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
BiblicalSignificance: The seal of a second prince named in Jeremiah 38:1 survives from Zedekiah's Jerusalem, confirming the Bible's account of the officials who moved against Jeremiah.

Description: An Aramaic retelling of the Genesis patriarchal stories, covering Lamech, Noah and Abraham, and one of the original seven Dead Sea Scrolls found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1946–1947. It survives on four sheets of leather and is the least well-preserved of the original seven, partly because its metallic ink has eaten into the parchment. Suggested dates for its composition range from the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD; it is a pseudepigraphal retelling, not a canonical book.
Interpretations: The Apocryphon shows how Second Temple Jews retold and expanded Genesis, filling narrative gaps (for example Lamech's doubts about Noah's birth and Abraham's meeting with Melchizedek) in the first person. It confirms that Genesis traditions circulated in expanded Aramaic forms before the New Testament period, but it is not Scripture and its expansions must not be treated as historical fact beyond Genesis itself.
AlternativeNames: Tales of the Patriarchs;Apocalypse of Lamech;1QapGen
BiblicalSignificance: It illuminates how Genesis was read, retold and treasured in the Second Temple period, and it preserves early Jewish traditions about Noah and Abraham found nowhere else.
ArtifactDate: 1st century BC–1st century AD (copy); composition suggested 3rd century BC–1st century AD
CurrentLocation: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem

Description: The Great Isaiah Scroll is the only complete biblical book found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, containing all 66 chapters of Isaiah in Hebrew on 17 sheets of parchment sewn together into a single scroll about 24 feet long. It was found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947 by Bedouin shepherds and was among the first seven scrolls recovered. Paleography dates the copy to about 125 BC, roughly a thousand years older than the medieval Masoretic codices. Its text agrees closely with the later Masoretic Text, with over 2,600 mostly minor variants of spelling and grammar.
Interpretations: The scroll is the strongest single witness to the stability of the Hebrew text of Isaiah across a thousand years: the book readers know today is essentially the book copied before the time of Christ. Its variants are mostly orthographic, but a few are theologically interesting, such as Isaiah 53:11, where the scroll adds the word 'light' ('he shall see light'). Because it predates Jesus, it also confirms that Isaiah 53 and the other messianic passages were written before the events Christians see them fulfilled in, not composed afterwards.
BiblicalSignificance: It proves the book of Isaiah was copied faithfully for over a thousand years, and that its prophecies, including Isaiah 53, existed in full more than a century before Jesus.
CurrentLocation: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem

Description: The Great Psalms Scroll, 11Q5 or 11QPsa, was found in Qumran Cave 11 in 1956 and is dated to about AD 30-50. It contains roughly 50 compositions, including about 40 canonical psalms arranged in a strikingly different order from the traditional Psalter, mostly from Psalms 101-150, plus eight non-Masoretic compositions. Among its extras are Psalm 151 in Hebrew, previously known only from the Greek Septuagint, and a prose list called 'David's Compositions' crediting David with thousands of songs.
Interpretations: The scroll challenges the idea that the Psalter's order and contents were fixed early: a first-century community used a Psalms collection ordered differently and containing pieces outside the traditional 150. Its Hebrew Psalm 151 confirms that the Greek psalm had a Hebrew original, and its 'David's Compositions' shows how David's reputation as psalmist and sage was celebrated at Qumran. The scroll's order is not evidence that the traditional Psalter is wrong; it is evidence that more than one arrangement circulated, and the traditional arrangement is the one that endured in Jewish and Christian Bibles.
ScriptureIlluminated: Psalms 101; Psalms 102; Psalms 103; Psalms 104; Psalms 105; Psalms 118; Psalms 119; Psalms 121; Psalms 122; Psalms 123; Psalms 124; Psalms 125; Psalms 126; Psalms 127; Psalms 128; Psalms 129; Psalms 130; Psalms 131; Psalms 132; Psalms 133; Psalms 134; Psalms 135; Psalms 136; Psalms 137; Psalms 138; Psalms 139; Psalms 140; Psalms 141; Psalms 142; Psalms 143; Psalms 144; Psalms 145; Psalms 146; Psalms 147; Psalms 148; Psalms 149; Psalms 150; 2 Samuel 23:1-7
BiblicalSignificance: It proves the Psalter's shape was still fluid in the first century and recovers the Hebrew original of Psalm 151, known before only in Greek.

Description: The Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, Rahlfs 943) is a Greek revision of the Old Greek translation of the Twelve Prophets, dated to about 50 BC-AD 50. Fragments first reached scholars through Bedouin in 1952, and nine more fragments were excavated in 1960-1961 from Cave 8, the 'Cave of Horror,' at Nahal Hever in the Judean Desert. Surviving portions cover Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Zechariah, with the Haggai portion lost. The scroll writes the divine name in paleo-Hebrew script within the Greek text.
Interpretations: The scroll belongs to the kaige recension (also called Proto-Theodotion), a Greek revision that brings the Old Greek closer to the Hebrew text, and it stands closer to the Masoretic Text than the later Christian copies of the Septuagint. It is therefore key evidence that Greek-speaking Jews were already revising their Bible toward the Hebrew in the first century, before Christian scribes standardized the Septuagint text. Its preservation of the Tetragrammaton in paleo-Hebrew letters, where Christian codices later wrote 'Lord,' shows how the divine name was handled before that change.
RelatedBooks: Jonah; Micah; Nahum; Habakkuk; Zephaniah; Zechariah
ScriptureIlluminated: Jonah 1-4; Micah 1-7; Nahum 1-3; Habakkuk 1-3; Zephaniah 1-3; Zechariah 1-14
BiblicalSignificance: It is the clearest evidence that the Greek Bible was revised toward the Hebrew before Christianity, and that the earliest Greek copies kept God's name in Hebrew letters.

Description: The Habakkuk Commentary, 1QpHab or Pesher Habakkuk, is a verse-by-verse commentary on Habakkuk 1-2 from Qumran Cave 1, found in 1947 as one of the original seven scrolls. Written in Herodian script in the second half of the 1st century BC, it runs to 13 columns of parchment about 1.48 meters long. Each quoted verse is followed by an interpretation introduced by the word 'pishro' ('its meaning'), applying the prophecy to the commentator's own time.
Interpretations: The commentary is the best window into how the Qumran community read prophecy: as a coded message about their own days, with the Teacher of Righteousness receiving the true meaning, the Wicked Priest and the Man of Lies as opponents, and the Kittim (understood as the Romans) as the invading Chaldeans of Habakkuk's day. The identities of the Teacher and Wicked Priest are never given by name, so they remain unidentified. Its quoted text of Habakkuk sometimes differs from the Masoretic Text, making it a textual witness for Habakkuk 1-2 as well as a commentary; note that the divine name is written in paleo-Hebrew script, unlike the rest of the text.
BiblicalSignificance: It shows how Jews before Christ read Habakkuk as prophecy about their own generation, and its quotations give an independent witness to the text of Habakkuk 1-2.

Description: A letter-like sectarian work reconstructed as a composite from six fragmentary Cave 4 manuscripts (4Q394–399), found between 1953 and 1959 and now in the Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem. It is one of the earliest Qumran sect works, with the original dated by some reconstructions to about 150 BC. It has four parts — a lost opening, a 364-day calendar, more than 20 rulings (halakhot) on Temple ritual and purity, and an epilogue urging separation from 'the multitude' and persuading the addressee — and it argues that disagreement on these rulings caused the sect's separation.
Interpretations: 4QMMT is the earliest evidence of the sect's legal disputes with the Jerusalem establishment, and its phrase 'works of the Torah' matches Paul's 'works of the law' (Galatians 2:16; 3:10; Romans 3:20, 28). The letter says righteousness will be 'reckoned' to those who do what is right, which illuminates but does not settle Paul's argument: the letter's author and Paul use similar language to opposite ends, and the parallel must not be flattened into agreement.
AlternativeNames: Miqsat Ma'ase ha-Torah;Some of the Works of the Torah;Some Precepts of the Torah;MMT
BiblicalSignificance: It is the closest Second Temple parallel to Paul's 'works of the law' language, and it anchors the New Testament's debates about law and righteousness in a real, datable Jewish dispute.

Description: The mosaic floor of the second synagogue at Hammat Tiberias, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee south of Tiberias, excavated by Moshe Dothan in 1961-1963. Dated to the second half of the 4th century AD, it is the earliest known synagogue mosaic pavement. Its three panels show a Torah shrine flanked by menorahs and ritual objects, a zodiac wheel around Helios with nine of the twelve signs surviving and the four seasons in the corners, and Greek donor inscriptions flanked by lions, including one naming Severus, pupil of the Patriarchs, which gives the building its name, the Synagogue of Severus. The synagogue was destroyed by an earthquake in the early 5th century.
Interpretations: Like Beit Alpha, this floor shows zodiac and Helios imagery inside a synagogue, so it illuminates the visual world of late-antique Judaism rather than biblical practice. The uncircumcised figure of Libra has led some scholars to suggest a non-Jewish artist. The donor inscriptions show a synagogue community organised enough to record its patrons in Greek beside its Hebrew heritage.
AlternativeNames: Hamat Tiberias Synagogue Mosaic; Synagogue of Severus Mosaic
BiblicalSignificance: The floor illuminates the Jewish world of the centuries after the New Testament, when synagogue worship continued around Torah, menorah and donor inscriptions in a Roman-Byzantine visual language.
ArtifactDate: Second half of the 4th century AD
CurrentLocation: In situ, Hamat Tiberias National Park, Israel
DiscoveryLocation: Hammat Tiberias, south of Tiberias, Israel
ImageCredit: Photo: Shlomo Roded / PikiWiki Israel (CC BY 2.5)

Description: A seal ring published in 1980, bearing a three-line paleo-Hebrew inscription in reverse letters, as usual for a seal, reading '(Belonging) to Hanan, son (of) Hilkiah the priest'. Hilkiah was the high priest under King Josiah who found the Book of the Law in the Temple (2 Kings 22:8). Hanan himself is not named in Scripture; the seal attests a priestly son of the biblical high priest in the late 7th century BC. Unlike the Azariah bulla of 1982, this seal does not come from the stratified City of David hoard, so it carries less archaeological weight than that bulla.
Interpretations: The seal names the biblical high priest Hilkiah as the father of a priest, Hanan, giving a second extra-biblical witness to Hilkiah's family alongside the Azariah bulla, and the two seals appear to be the work of the same engraver. Because Hanan is not himself a biblical figure and the seal lacks the Azariah bulla's stratified context, the entry claims the Hilkiah connection, not a biblical identity for Hanan.
BiblicalSignificance: A priest's seal naming Hilkiah as his father corroborates the high priest of Josiah's reform from a second object, complementing the Azariah bulla found in Jerusalem.

Description: A Hebron limestone stele, 110 by 57.5 cm, inscribed in Koine Greek and dated to 178 BCE (Seleucid year 134, month Gorpiaios). It preserves a dossier of three letters: King Seleucus IV Philopator writes to his chief minister Heliodorus appointing Olympiodorus over the sanctuaries of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, and the order is forwarded down the chain to Dorymenes and then Diophanes. The main part reached the Israel Museum via the antiquities market (acquired by Michael Steinhardt in 2007), while three further fragments were found in licensed excavations at subterranean complex 57, Maresha, in 2005-2006 and joined to it.
Interpretations: PROVENANCE AND CONTENT CAUTIONS: the main part of the stele came through the antiquities trade and was among 180 looted artefacts Steinhardt agreed to surrender to the Manhattan District Attorney in December 2021, though its authenticity was confirmed by patina and soil analysis and by the Maresha fragments. The stele confirms Heliodorus as a real historical figure, but it names Olympiodorus, not Heliodorus, as sanctuary overseer - so it does NOT directly confirm the 2 Maccabees 3 episode in which Heliodorus tries to seize the Jerusalem temple treasury; scholars explain the gap either by Olympiodorus's oversight provoking Heliodorus's intervention, or by 2 Maccabees substituting the more famous minister. EvidenceClass is therefore Contextual, not Direct.
BiblicalSignificance: The stele illuminates the Seleucid pressure on temple treasuries that forms the background to 2 Maccabees 3 and to the persecution under Antiochus IV; no canonical passage is cited because 2 Maccabees is outside the 66-book Protestant canon used on this site.
DiscoveryLocation: Maresha, Israel (subterranean complex 57); main fragments via the antiquities market

Description: Bronze prutahs of Herod Agrippa I, king of Judaea (ruled AD 37-44; king of Judaea from AD 41), struck at the Jerusalem mint. The year 6 issue (AD 41/42, under Claudius) shows a fringed umbrella-like canopy with the Greek inscription 'of King Agrippa' and, on the reverse, three ears of barley with the date L Ϛ flanking (Hendin 1244; Meshorer TJC 120; RPC I 4981; British Museum example 1908,0110.376, 17 mm, 2.34 g). For non-Jewish areas he also struck portrait and pagan types, including issues with Caligula.
Interpretations: The coins name King Agrippa — the 'Herod' of Acts 12 who had James put to death and Peter imprisoned. The canopy is read as a symbol of royal power and the barley as the land's fertility; those readings are conventional, not inscribed. The aniconic Jerusalem type contrasts with his portrait issues for Gentile areas, showing the same dual policy as his grandfather's coinage.
BiblicalSignificance: Acts 12:1-4 opens with 'Herod the king' arresting church members, killing James and seizing Peter; these coins name that king, struck at Jerusalem in AD 41/42, just before those events.
CurrentLocation: British Museum (example 1908,0110.376); other examples widely held

Description: Bronze coins of Herod Agrippa II, the last Herodian ruler (reigned AD 50-c. 100), the most extensive and most problematic of the Herodian coinages because dating by his regnal eras is complex (the common view uses an era starting AD 60/61). Flavian-era denominations pair imperial portraits with fixed reverses: the largest shows Vespasian with the Tyche of Caesarea Philippi, the middle Titus with Nike advancing holding wreath and palm, and the smallest Domitian with Nike writing on a shield (years 14, 15, 18). Earlier issues include a palm-branch coin struck at Tiberias in AD 53 and portrait issues under Nero.
Interpretations: The coinage is Agrippa's — the king before whom Paul defended himself in Acts 25-26 — though many issues name only the emperor, with Agrippa's name on the reverse. The Nike iconography echoes the Roman Iudea Capta series, but Meshorer argues Agrippa did not intend to celebrate his own people's defeat; the victory celebrated is the Flavian victory in the civil war. Regnal-era dating remains debated, so year attributions carry that caution.
BiblicalSignificance: Acts 25:13 records Agrippa's arrival at Caesarea to greet Festus, leading to Paul's defense before him in Acts 26; these are the coins of that king, struck across the decades of the early church's growth.

Description: Bronze coins of Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea (4 BC-AD 39), struck at the Tiberias mint in four denominations (eight units to a denarius). The first series (year 24 = AD 20/21) names the city 'Tiberias' in Greek within a wreath on one side with a reed on the other — the first Jewish coinage to name a city. Middle series (years 33, 34, 37 = AD 29/30, 30/31, 33/34) pair 'Tiberias' in a wreath with a palm branch inscribed 'Herod the Tetrarch'; the final series is year 43 (AD 39). No series carries portraits or figural images.
Interpretations: The coins name Herod the Tetrarch and his capital Tiberias, and their avoidance of graven images — unusual for a ruler of his time — shows deference to the Jewish ban on images, matching the picture of a ruler balancing Jewish and Roman worlds. Antipas issued only five series in 43 years, and none before his 24th regnal year, suggesting a light footprint in Galilee.
BiblicalSignificance: Mark 6 names 'king Herod' hearing of Jesus and recalls his execution of John the Baptist; these are the coins of that tetrarch, struck at Tiberias in the very years of John's death and Jesus' ministry.

Description: Bronze prutahs of Herod Archelaus, ethnarch of Judaea, Samaria, and Idumaea (4 BC-AD 6), struck at the Jerusalem mint. Types include a double cornucopia with grapes paired with a war galley showing aphlaston, oars, and ram; grapes paired with a crested helmet; and an anchor paired with a wreath inscribed EΘN (Ethnarch). Inscriptions in Greek read 'of Herod' and 'of the Ethnarch'; there are no portraits, in deference to Jewish sensitivities. The galley type recalls his voyage to Rome to appeal for his father's kingdom after Herod's will was changed.
Interpretations: The coins name Herod the Ethnarch, the ruler Matthew 2:22 says Joseph feared on returning from Egypt. The galley's allusion to the Rome voyage is a scholarly reading of the imagery, not an inscriptional statement.
BiblicalSignificance: When Joseph heard that Archelaus reigned in Judaea in place of his father Herod, 'he was afraid to go thither' (Matthew 2:22) and turned aside into Galilee; these coins name the ethnarch whose reign prompted that fear.

Description: Bronze prutahs and half-prutahs (lepta) of Herod the Great, struck at the Jerusalem mint during his reign (king from 37 BC; ruled 40-4 BC). The most common type pairs an anchor inscribed 'of King Herod' in Greek with a double cornucopia and caduceus (Meshorer TJC 59; struck in huge quantities, c. 21-12 BC). Other types include a cornucopia with an eagle — the first coin by a Jewish ruler to carry a graven image, linked to the golden eagle Herod set over the Temple gate c. 4 BC — and an anchor with a galley, possibly recalling the harbor at Caesarea Maritima (built 22-10 BC).
Interpretations: The coins name 'King Herod' — the Matthew 2 ruler — in Greek. Their symbolism is debated: some read the anchor and cornucopiae as continuing Hasmonean types, others as pagan or sovereignty imagery, so do not overclaim a single reading. The eagle type's connection to the Temple-gate eagle is a plausible link, not a certainty. The coinage as a whole shows a ruler balancing Jewish sensibilities (no portraits) with Hellenistic royal imagery.
BiblicalSignificance: Matthew 2 opens 'in the days of Herod the king'; these are the coins of that king, struck in Jerusalem in the years around Jesus' birth, and they name him directly.
CurrentLocation: Examples in the Israel Museum and the British Museum

Description: Ink-inscribed potsherds from Tell Hesban (biblical Heshbon), excavated by Siegfried Horn's Heshbon Expedition (1968-1970s seasons) from reservoir fill. Written in Ammonite language and script of the 7th-6th centuries BC, the group documents Ammonite administration at Heshbon; Ostracon IV, an 11-line economic text studied by Frank Cross, lists grain, cattle, flour, and wine delivered as tax, including 35 jars of grain plus 8 sheep or goats to the king.
HistoricalPeriod: Iron Age II to Persian transition; 7th-6th century BC
Interpretations: The ostraca show Heshbon under Ammonite administration after passing from Moabite to Ammonite control, and attest a functioning tax system in the southern Levant on the eve of the exile. Cautions: the ostraca are 7th-6th-century Ammonite documents, NOT from the time of Sihon, king of the Amorites, whose capital Heshbon was (Numbers 21), so Sihon is deliberately not linked as a person; the site's large plastered pool is sometimes linked to the 'pools of Heshbon' of Song of Solomon 7:4, but that link is a possibility, not a proof, and the archaeology is explicitly silent on a Sihon-era battle at Heshbon.
BiblicalSignificance: They document Ammonite administration at biblical Heshbon centuries after Sihon, showing the city's long later history, while the Sihon-era and pools connections remain site associations, not proofs.

Description: The Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty, also called the Eternal Treaty or Silver Treaty, concluded around 1259 BC between Ramesses II of Egypt and Hattusili III of the Hittites after the Battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) and decades of war. It is the oldest known surviving peace treaty and the only ancient Near Eastern treaty preserved in versions from both parties: the Egyptian version engraved in hieroglyphs on the walls of the Ramesseum and the Precinct of Amun-Re at Karnak, and the Akkadian version on clay tablets excavated at Hattusa in 1906-1912 by Hugo Winckler. Its terms cover non-aggression, mutual defense, recognition of sovereignty, and extradition of fugitives; the original silver tablets have not survived, and a replica hangs at United Nations headquarters.
