Description: The port city of the Troad, called simply Troas in Acts, sprawling over some 400 hectares with baths, an odeon, a theatre, a gymnasium, and a circuit of walls some ten kilometres long. From Troas Paul sailed for Europe after the Macedonian vision of Acts 16:9-11, and there on his return journey he preached until midnight in an upper room, Eutychus fell asleep, dropped three stories, and was taken up dead — until Paul embraced him and said his life was in him. Paul later asked Timothy to bring the cloak, books, and parchments he had left at Troas.
Interpretations: The site's identification is certain and its scale matches a major port, but no building at Troas is identified with the upper room of Acts 20:7-12; the odeon and theatre are civic remains, not the meeting place. The entry claims the city, not a room.
BiblicalSignificance: Troas is the hinge of Acts: the place where the gospel turns from Asia to Europe. The Macedonian call, the first European converts at Philippi, and the breaking of bread at Troas with Eutychus's restoration all belong to this port. Its ruins — a harbour city built for traffic between continents — make the hinge visible.
ArtifactDate: Hellenistic foundation, Roman colony from Augustus; baths endowed AD 135
CurrentLocation: In situ, Alexandria Troas archaeological site

Description: The synagogue of Ostia, the port of Rome, discovered by chance in 1961 during roadworks for the Fiumicino airport link and excavated under Maria Floriani Squarciapino. Menorah-carved marble beams and menorah-stamped lamps announced the find: a main hall with benches, a Torah shrine donated by Mindus Faustus (inscription, 2nd-3rd century), and a later aedicula. It is the oldest synagogue yet found in Europe and the oldest mainstream synagogue uncovered outside Israel, in use into the 5th century.
Interpretations: The building's identification as a synagogue is secure, but its earliest date is debated: Squarciapino dated the first phase to the 1st century, while later scholars (notably L. Michael White) argue the building began as a house only later converted, with the certain synagogue phase in the 2nd century or later. The visible remains are mostly 4th century. No direct link to Paul or to any named Roman Christian is claimed.
BiblicalSignificance: Paul wrote to a church in Rome he had not founded, and Acts closes with him preaching in Rome 'with all confidence, no man forbidding him.' Ostia shows the Jewish world that church grew beside: a large, organised diaspora community at Rome's own harbour, with its own synagogue, Torah shrine, and communal life — the same world of synagogue and Scripture from which the Roman church drew its first members.
ArtifactDate: 1st century AD (earliest phase, debated); main remains 4th century AD
CurrentLocation: In situ, Ostia Antica archaeological park

Description: The 'queen of the catacombs' on the Via Salaria: some 13 kilometres of tufa galleries holding about 40,000 burials, including popes and martyrs of the Diocletian persecution. Rediscovered in the 16th century after centuries of oblivion and plundering, it still preserves the oldest known depiction of the Virgin Mary with the Child (late 2nd-early 3rd century, with Balaam pointing to a star), Good Shepherd frescoes, and the Greek Chapel's scenes of Moses, Isaac, Lazarus, and the Magi, with a Eucharistic banquet scene. The Priscilla after whom it is named was most probably a noblewoman of the senatorial Acilii family who donated the land — not certainly the Priscilla of Acts and Romans.
Interpretations: The art and its dates are secure, but two cautions apply: the Good Shepherd image also existed in pre-Christian Roman burial art, so individual images are read as Christian by context, not by the motif alone; and the namesake Priscilla is not identified with the New Testament Priscilla, so no profile link is made to her. The 'veiled woman' and banquet scenes are also debated in detail.
BiblicalSignificance: The catacombs show what the resurrection hope looked like to Christians who buried their dead under persecution: a shepherd carrying the sheep, a mother and child beneath a star, Lazarus raised, bread broken at a banquet table. They are the earliest Christian art we have, made by people who had to bury in secret and who painted their faith on the walls of their graves.

Description: The library of Ephesus, commissioned in the AD 110s by the consul Tiberius Julius Aquila as a funerary monument for his father, the former proconsul of Asia Tiberius Julius Celsus Polemaeanus, who is buried in a sarcophagus in a crypt beneath the hall. The third-largest library of the Greco-Roman world, it held about 12,000 scrolls; its two-storey marble facade, re-erected by anastylosis in 1970-1978, is now Ephesus's most recognisable building. It postdates Paul's ministry at Ephesus by half a century and is a different building from the Ephesus Theater already in this collection.
Interpretations: The building, its patron, and its scroll capacity are well documented; the facade statues visible today are replacements, and the interior and its scrolls were destroyed by fire in AD 262. The library does not date from Paul's time and no link to any New Testament event is claimed — it illuminates the city's later book culture, not the apostolic visit.
BiblicalSignificance: Ephesus was the city of Paul's longest ministry, of the riot of the silversmiths, and of the first of the seven letters. The library shows the book-world that city inhabited: a culture of scrolls, public reading, and monumental learning, in which the burning of the magic books in Acts 19:19 — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth of scrolls — was a costly and public break with the old wisdom.
ArtifactDate: AD 110s, completed under Hadrian; facade re-erected 1970-1978

Description: A silver denarius of Caesar Augustus (Octavian), first emperor of Rome, bearing his portrait and the legend CAESAR AVGVSTVS. Augustus's reign saw the empire's first systematic censuses, recorded in his own Res Gestae (28 BC, 8 BC, AD 14), and his coinage carried his image and titles into every province, including Judea, where his client king Herod ruled.
Interpretations: The coin type is genuine and ubiquitous; no claim is made that any particular denarius was handled in Judea at the census, and the exact registration Luke describes remains debated (notably the Quirinius question in Luke 2:2). The coin illustrates the emperor and his administration, not a proven census transaction.
BiblicalSignificance: Luke 2:1-5 opens the nativity with Augustus's decree 'that all the world should be taxed,' sending Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem and so fulfilling Micah 5:2 without Augustus knowing it. This is the face on the money of the man whose census moved the holy family — the emperor whose power, unknowingly, served God's purpose.
CurrentLocation: Examples in many museum collections, including the British Museum and the Metropolitan Museum of Art

Description: A silver tetradrachm of Alexander III of Macedon, about 17 grams: the obverse shows Heracles in a lion skin (on lifetime issues) or the deified Alexander wearing the horn of Ammon (on posthumous Lysimachus-type issues), the reverse Zeus enthroned holding an eagle. Alexander's coinage circulated across the empire he conquered in a decade and was copied by his successors for generations, spreading Greek language and culture — the world in which the New Testament would later be written.
Interpretations: The identification of Daniel 8's goat and horn with Greece and Alexander is the standard historical reading, shared across conservative and critical scholarship; debate concerns the date of Daniel's composition, not the identity of the figure. No claim is made that Daniel saw this coin type, which postdates the vision's setting.
BiblicalSignificance: Daniel 8 pictures Greece as a he-goat from the west whose 'notable horn' charges the Medo-Persian ram, and the interpretation is explicit: 'the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.' The great horn is Alexander; the horn broken at its height (Daniel 8:8) is his death at thirty-two, and the four horns that replace it are the four kingdoms of his successors. The tetradrachm is the face of that horn.
ArtifactDate: 336-323 BC (lifetime issues); posthumous issues into the 3rd century BC
CurrentLocation: Examples in many museum collections, including the Art Institute of Chicago

Description: A polished limestone dome weight of the full shekel standard, about 11.3-11.4 grams, of the kind found by the hundred in Jerusalem and Judah. Many carry their denomination engraved in ancient Hebrew script. Before coins reached Judah (about 600 BC), silver was weighed against such stones on balance scales: a shekel was a weight before it was a coin, and the full shekel is the unit of which the beka — already in this collection — is the half.
Interpretations: Shekel weights are well attested and their standard is agreed at about 11.3-11.4 grams, though individual examples vary slightly and the 'shekel of the sanctuary' may have differed marginally from the ordinary commercial shekel. This entry describes the type, not one single provenanced stone, and is deliberately distinct from the inscribed beka weight and pim weight already in the collection.
AlternativeNames: Full Shekel Stone Weight; Shekel of the Sanctuary Weight
BiblicalSignificance: The shekel is the Bible's standard of value from Genesis to the Temple tax: Abraham weighs four hundred shekels for Machpelah, Jeremiah weighs seventeen shekels for the field at Anathoth, and Exodus 30:13 fixes the sanctuary tax at half a shekel 'after the shekel of the sanctuary.' Holding the full weight makes the half-shekel of the beka, and every weighed payment in Scripture, a physical thing rather than an abstraction.
CurrentLocation: Examples in museum collections in Jerusalem

Description: The excavated agora of Smyrna, the Roman marketplace rebuilt under Faustina the Younger after the earthquake of AD 178: a large basilica, vaulted ground-floor halls, and colonnades, with the Roman theatre now also uncovered on the slope of Kadifekale. Most of ancient Smyrna lies under the modern city and cannot be dug, so the agora is the principal visible remnant of the city that received the second of the seven letters. Graffiti in the basilica's plaster, dated no later than AD 125, includes the isopsephic pairing 'Lord 800 / Faith 800.'
Interpretations: The agora's identity and rebuild date are secure, but the visible remains postdate John's letter (the rebuild follows AD 178), so they show Smyrna's later civic setting, not the first-century church's own buildings. Polycarp's martyrdom and its stadium setting rest on the Martyrdom of Polycarp, an early church document, not on archaeology. No profile link is made to Polycarp, who has no profile in the collection.
BiblicalSignificance: Smyrna's letter, Revelation 2:8-11, is the only one of the seven with no rebuke: a poor, slandered church told to be faithful unto death and promised the crown of life. The agora shows the prosperous, temple-crowded city in which that poverty and pressure were lived — and the generation after John, Smyrna's bishop Polycarp was martyred in its stadium, most likely in AD 155 or 156, living out the letter he had inherited.
CurrentLocation: In situ, Smyrna Agora Archaeological Park, Izmir

Description: A deep well, about 41 m in its present form, under a Greek Orthodox church near Shechem, venerated since at least the 4th century AD as the well where Jesus spoke with the Samaritan woman (John 4). A cruciform Byzantine church stood over it by AD 384; the well was used for baptisms by AD 333 according to the Bordeaux Pilgrim. The present church is 20th-century, over Byzantine remains. The well is not named in the Old Testament: Genesis records Jacob buying land at Shechem and giving a parcel to Joseph, but no well dug by Jacob is mentioned there.
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: this entry rests on standing tradition, not excavation. The present well shaft is Roman-period construction, the church tradition begins in the 4th century, and a nearer village spring ('Ain 'Askar) was the ordinary water source for Sychar's women — a point already noted by 19th-century commentators. The identification is therefore plausible and ancient as tradition, but not archaeologically proven, and the well must not be presented as certainly Jacob's own digging or certainly the well of John 4.
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob
BiblicalSignificance: If this is the well of John 4, it is where Jesus first told someone plainly that He is the Messiah (John 4:26), and where 'living water' was offered to an outsider — a Samaritan woman — before any of it was offered in Jerusalem. That is why the tradition has been guarded for seventeen centuries, even though the archaeology cannot prove the identification.
ArtifactDate: Roman period (present well shaft); Byzantine church 4th century AD
CurrentLocation: In situ, crypt of the Greek Orthodox Church of Jacob's Well, Nablus, West Bank
DateDiscovered: Tradition attested by the 4th century AD (Bordeaux Pilgrim, AD 333; church by AD 384)
DiscoveryLocation: Near Shechem (Nablus), between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, West Bank

Description: Three large stepped reservoirs in the Artas Valley, each about 6 m lower than the one above, partly rock-hewn and partly built of large hewn stones, with a combined capacity of roughly 230,000-340,000 cubic metres. Fed by springs, runoff and feeder aqueducts, they supplied Jerusalem's water for over 2,000 years: the Low-Level Aqueduct carried their water to cisterns beneath the Temple Mount in the late Second Temple period, the High-Level Aqueduct ran toward the Upper City, and a branch supplied Herodium. An Ottoman fortress (Murad Castle, 1618) guarded them. No verse names these pools.
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: the name is traditional, not historical. Scholars date the oldest pool to the 2nd century BC, with Herodian and later phases — centuries after Solomon. The link to Ecclesiastes 2:6 ('I made me pools of water') is a traditional association via Josephus's picture of Solomon strolling in gardens here, not an identification: the verse names no place, and these pools cannot be Solomon's. The pools' Second Temple function as Jerusalem's water supply is, by contrast, well established.
AlternativeNames: Burak Sulayman; Breichot Shlomo; Pools of Artas
BiblicalSignificance: The pools are the hidden infrastructure of Temple Jerusalem: without reservoirs and aqueducts like these, the pilgrim city of the Gospels could not have drunk, washed or sacrificed at scale. They illuminate the water world behind the Temple courts — the cisterns, pools and washings of Second Temple worship — even though their Solomonic name is traditional, not historical.
ArtifactDate: c. 2nd century BC (oldest pool) - early Roman period (aqueduct masonry)
CurrentLocation: In situ, near al-Khader, West Bank
DateDiscovered: Known since antiquity; surveyed and studied in modern times
DiscoveryLocation: Artas Valley, about 3.5 km south-west of Bethlehem, West Bank

FindName: Pasargadae and the Tomb of Cyrus
Description: The first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BC on the Morghab plain in southern Iran. Its excavated remains include audience halls, palaces, pavilions, and formal gardens, and, about a kilometre from the palaces, a small stepped limestone tomb with a gabled chamber, standing about 11 metres tall. Classical writers (Arrian, following Aristobulus, and Strabo) describe Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae in matching terms, and the structure was long called the Tomb of the Mother of Solomon before James Morier reattributed it to Cyrus in 1812. No inscription naming Cyrus survives on the tomb, and some scholars note the attribution rests on the classical accounts rather than on an inscription found in place.
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: Pasargadae itself is securely Cyrus's capital, but the tomb's identification as Cyrus's own burial place is traditional, resting on classical descriptions and on Morier's 1812 reattribution, not on a surviving inscription; the tomb was also attributed for centuries to the Mother of Solomon. The entry is therefore borderline, not clear: the capital is certain, the tomb attribution is not proven.
AlternativeNames: Tomb of Cyrus; Tomb of the Mother of Solomon (former attribution)
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
BiblicalSignificance: Cyrus is the king Isaiah named before his birth and Ezra credits with the decree that sent the exiles home. Pasargadae is the capital he built, and the tomb in its park is the monument classical writers describe as his — but the tomb's own inscription is lost, so this entry claims the tradition and the archaeology, not a proven burial.
CurrentLocation: In situ, Pasargadae, Fars Province, Iran (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
DateDiscovered: Identified as Cyrus's capital by Ernst Herzfeld, 1908 (site known to travellers earlier)

Description: The oldest royal capital of united Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile where the valley opens into the Delta, about 20 km south of modern Cairo, at the modern village of Mit Rahina. Tradition credits its founding to Menes around 3000 BC, and for most of three thousand years it was a chief city of Egypt and a centre of the worship of Ptah and the Apis bull. Compared with its cemeteries at Saqqara and Giza, the city itself has yielded few visible remains: Petrie worked the Ptah temple precinct and the palace of Apries, later expeditions found the palace of Merneptah, and the most famous surviving monument is the colossal fallen statue of Ramesses II. The prophets call the city Noph (once Moph in Hosea), eight times in all, chiefly in oracles of judgment against Egypt and in connection with Jews who settled there after Jerusalem's fall.
HistoricalPeriod: Old Kingdom to Late Period, Egypt
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED (thin excavation, per brief): the identification of Mit Rahina with biblical Memphis/Noph is broadly accepted, but the city itself is largely gone — its remains are scatters, temple precincts, and palaces, with no excavated structure tied to a specific biblical event, and the Ramesses statue pictured is a general monument of the city, not an object from a biblical episode. Borderline rather than clear for that reason.
BiblicalSignificance: Memphis is the city the prophets name when Egypt itself is judged: its princes deceived, its idols to cease, its people to bury the fugitives who fled there. The prophets' Memphis is a real capital, not a symbol — but its excavated city remains are thin, and no excavated structure is tied to a specific biblical event, so this entry stays borderline.
ArtifactDate: Founded c. 3000 BC (tradition); occupied for some 3,000 years
CurrentLocation: In situ, Mit Rahina, Egypt (open-air museum; colossal Ramesses II statue on site)
DateDiscovered: Excavated by Flinders Petrie, 1908-1913 (site identified earlier)

Description: One of the oldest and most important cities of southern Mesopotamia, at modern Nuffar southeast of Babylon, dominated by the great temple-tower of E-kur, the temple of Enlil, god of the air and chief of the Sumerian pantheon. The University of Pennsylvania expedition begun by J. P. Peters in 1889 uncovered the temple, the ziggurat, residential quarters, and tens of thousands of tablets, making Nippur a cornerstone of Sumerian literature and religion. George Rawlinson proposed Nippur as biblical Calneh, the fourth city of Nimrod's kingdom in Genesis 10:10, citing the Talmudic name Nopher; other scholars prefer Kul-unu, a site near Babylon, or Hursagkalama near Kish, and one recent proposal even reads Calneh as Kalhu (Nimrud). The name Calneh's cuneiform equivalent remains doubtful.
HistoricalPeriod: Sumerian to Parthian, 3rd millennium BC onwards
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: Nippur's own archaeology is secure, but its equation with biblical Calneh is disputed — Rawlinson's Nippur proposal competes with Kul-unu and Hursagkalama, and with a Kalhu reading. ScriptureIlluminated (Genesis 10:10) therefore applies only if the Nippur proposal is right, and the entry is borderline for that reason.
BiblicalSignificance: If Nippur is Calneh, it is one of the four founding cities of Nimrod's kingdom in Genesis 10:10 — the religious heart of Sumer, seat of Enlil, whose archives shaped our knowledge of the world Abraham left. But the identification is only one of several proposals, so the illumination is conditional, and this entry stays borderline.
ArtifactDate: Occupied from c. 5000 BC; ziggurat and temple of Enlil, 3rd-2nd millennium BC
DateDiscovered: American excavations begun by J. P. Peters, 1889-1900

Description: The capital of the Median kingdom and later a summer capital and treasury city of the Achaemenid and Parthian empires, at modern Hamadan on the slopes of Mount Alvand in western Iran, on the Royal Road between Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau. Its identification with Hamadan is considered secure on historical and archaeological grounds, and the Nabonidus Chronicle records Cyrus's capture of the city and its treasures in 550 BC. But excavation has always been restricted because the modern city covers most of the ancient settlement: work on Hagmatana hill has produced column bases, capitals, and scattered Achaemenid objects, but the Median palace, the treasury, and the royal archive of Ezra 6:2 have not been identified as buildings. Ezra 6:2 is the city's only explicit biblical reference, naming it Achmetha, where the memorandum of Cyrus's temple decree was found.
HistoricalPeriod: Median to Sasanian, 7th century BC onwards
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED (thin excavation, per brief): the city identification (Hamadan = Ecbatana = Achmetha) is secure, but the visible remains are thin and the archive building of Ezra 6:2 is not identified; Herodotus's seven coloured walls are a Greek construction, not an excavated reality. Borderline rather than clear because the biblical link rests on the city's identity and function, not on an excavated structure.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
BiblicalSignificance: Ecbatana is where the search for Cyrus's decree ended: the archives of Babylon yielded nothing, but the record found at Achmetha in Media confirmed the exiles' right to rebuild. That single verse anchors the return from exile in a real imperial filing system — but the archive building itself has never been identified, so this entry stays borderline.
ArtifactDate: Median capital from 7th century BC; Achaemenid summer capital, 6th-4th centuries BC
CurrentLocation: In situ, beneath modern Hamadan, Iran (Hagmatana hill partly excavated; UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2024)
DateDiscovered: Excavation begun 1913 under Charles Fossey; systematic work from 1983

Description: An ancient city of Sumer about 18 km southwest of Babylon, whose temple of Nabu, Ezida, and its staged tower still rise about 50 metres above the plain at Birs Nimrud — one of the most vividly identifiable surviving ziggurats. Rawlinson uncovered foundation prisms of Nebuchadnezzar II's restoration of the Nabu temple, and Rassam concentrated on Ezida itself; some two thousand tablets were later looted from the temple. Nebuchadnezzar's inscription describes the tower of Borsippa as an ancient work whose top had fallen to ruin and which he restored, and later Talmudic and Arabic tradition identified the ruin with the Tower of Babel. Modern scholarship concludes the builders raised it as a religious edifice for Nabu, the son of Babylon's Marduk, as befitted Babylon's lesser sister-city.
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: the ziggurat and its identity as Nabu's Ezida tower are secure, but its identification with the Genesis 11 tower is traditional only — the rival traditional candidate, Etemenanki at Babylon, is already entry #228, and modern scholarship assigns Borsippa's tower to Nabu. Borderline rather than clear because the biblical illumination (Genesis 11:1-9) depends on that unproven tradition.
BiblicalSignificance: Borsippa's ruined ziggurat is the most striking tower still standing in Babylonia, and Jewish and Arabic tradition has long called it the Tower of Babel — Nebuchadnezzar's own inscription calls it the tower of Borsippa, left unfinished by a former king. Modern scholarship reads it as the temple-tower of Nabu, not the Genesis tower, so the Babel link is tradition only, and this entry stays borderline.
ArtifactDate: Temple of Nabu (Ezida) restored by Nebuchadnezzar II, 6th century BC; earlier stages older
CurrentLocation: In situ, Birs Nimrud, Babylon Governorate, Iraq
DateDiscovered: Worked by Henry Rawlinson, 1854; excavated by Hormuzd Rassam, 1879-1881

Description: The form of the five books of Moses preserved by the Samaritan community, in Samaritan script resembling Paleo-Hebrew, with about six thousand variant readings against the Masoretic Text, including the command to worship on Mount Gerizim. Its most venerated copy, the Abisha Scroll at Nablus, claims in its own cryptogram to have been written by Abisha, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, in the thirteenth year after Israel entered Canaan. Modern study shows the scroll is a composite of sections from different periods, patched over time, with its oldest portions dating to the medieval period, around the 11th or 12th century AD.
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: the Abisha Scroll's claim to Aaron's great-grandson as author is Samaritan tradition, not a historical date, and cannot be substantiated; scholars date its oldest portions to the 11th-12th century AD. The text tradition itself is real and ancient, but any entry built on the scroll must not present the Abisha dating as fact. No manuscript of the Samaritan Pentateuch is older than the tenth century.
BiblicalSignificance: As an independent textual tradition, the Samaritan Pentateuch is a genuine third witness alongside the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, and Dead Sea Scrolls of a pre-Samaritan text-type show its roots reach back before Christ. Its Gerizim reading is also the direct background to the Samaritan woman's question in John 4 about the right mountain for worship.
ArtifactDate: c. 11th-12th century AD (oldest portions of the Abisha Scroll; tradition older)
CurrentLocation: Samaritan synagogue, Nablus; other manuscripts in libraries worldwide
DateDiscovered: Unknown (in continuous Samaritan custody at Nablus)

Description: A Phoenician inscribed stone (KAI 46), about 3.5 feet high, found at Nora on Sardinia's south coast in 1773 and now in Cagliari. It is the oldest Phoenician inscription found outside the Levant. Its eight surviving lines name a Phoenician general, Milkaton son of Shubna, and a king Pummay, but the top of the stone is broken or disputed, and the first surviving line is read by some scholars as 'at Tarshish' (btršš) and by others as two words meaning 'a house he beat down'.
Interpretations: DOUBT STATED: the Tarshish reading is disputed, not settled. Frank Moore Cross read the first line as 'at Tarshish' and identified Pummay with Pygmalion of Tyre, but other scholars divide the line differently and read the text as a temple-foundation or conquest record without Tarshish, and the stone was not found in its primary context, so no find context can settle the reading. The entry must present Tarshish as a proposed reading, not a fact.
RelatedPeople: King Solomon; Jonah; Hiram, King of Tyre
BiblicalSignificance: If the Tarshish reading is right, the stone would put the Bible's Tarshish, the distant source of silver in Solomon's and Jonah's day, in the western Mediterranean world of Phoenician trade, with Sardinia as a candidate alongside Spain. The stone certainly proves a Phoenician presence in Sardinia by the ninth century BC, the same seafaring network that carried Solomon's ships.

Description: A limestone ossuary from a rock-cut family tomb in the Kidron Valley, excavated in 1941 by Eleazar Sukenik and Nahman Avigad, inscribed in Greek 'Alexander (son) of Simon' and on the lid in Greek 'of Alexander' with the Hebrew letters QRNYT, read as 'the Cyrenian.' Mark 15:21 names Simon of Cyrene as 'the father of Alexander and Rufus,' as though his readers would know the sons. DOUBT STATED: Simon and Alexander were both very common names, the tomb held no ossuary for Rufus, and the identification cannot be proven. What is certain is a Cyrenian Jewish family buried in Jerusalem before AD 70; whether its Alexander is Mark's Alexander is proposed, not established.
Interpretations: Scholars divide: some (Lemaire, and recently Johnston) call the identification serious or likely, noting that this is the only known 'Alexander son of Simon' ossuary and that the Cyrene tag adds specificity; others stress the commonness of both names and the missing Rufus, and treat it as suggestive only. The ossuary itself is authentic; only the link to Mark 15:21 is disputed, and this entry is placed in BORDERLINE for that reason.
RelatedPeople: Simon of Cyrene; Alexander, Son of Simon of Cyrene; Rufus, Son of Simon of Cyrene; Jesus
BiblicalSignificance: If the identification were right, this would be the bone box of a man whose father carried Jesus's cross — and whose family, by Mark's way of naming him, was known to the first readers of the Gospel. Even without the identification, the ossuary confirms the world Mark describes: Cyrenian Jews living and buried in Jerusalem, exactly as Acts 6:9 records a synagogue of Cyrenians.
CurrentLocation: In storage, Israel Antiquities Authority collections (not on public display)
DiscoveryLocation: Kidron Valley burial cave, Jerusalem, Israel

Description: A rock-cut family tomb found during construction in East Talpiot in 1980 and excavated by Amos Kloner for the Israel Antiquities Authority, containing ten ossuaries, six inscribed: 'Yeshua bar Yehosef' (Jesus son of Joseph), 'Maria,' 'Yose,' 'Mariamne e Mara,' 'Yehuda bar Yeshua' (Judah son of Jesus), and one partially illegible. A 2007 documentary and book claimed this was the family tomb of Jesus of Nazareth. DOUBT STATED, IN FULL: every one of these names was extremely common in first-century Judea; 'Mariamne' has no established link to Mary Magdalene (the Acts of Philip connection is speculation); the excavator himself rejected the identification; the statistical case has been widely debunked; and the claim contradicts the Gospel accounts of Jesus's burial and resurrection and all early Christian tradition about it. The scholarly consensus, voiced by Geza Vermes and Jodi Magness among others, is that the 'Jesus family tomb' theory is sensational and without scientific basis. The tomb itself is genuine; the identification is not accepted.
Interpretations: The ossuaries are authentic first-century boxes and their inscriptions are real; what is disputed is everything built on them. No reputable case survives the commonness of the names, the unsupported Mariamne-Magdalene equation, and the contradiction with the burial narratives. This entry must never be presented as a candidate family tomb of Jesus without the doubt above.
AlternativeNames: Talpiyot Tomb; Jesus Family Tomb (disputed claim)
RelatedPeople: Jesus; Mary Magdalene; Joseph of Arimathea
BiblicalSignificance: Included in BORDERLINE only so readers meet the claim with its refutation attached: the tomb is the most famous cautionary case in biblical archaeology, showing why a cluster of common names is not an identification. Its proper illumination is negative — it clarifies, by contrast, what the Gospels actually record about Jesus's burial in a new tomb (Matthew 27:57-60) and his empty tomb on the third day.
CurrentLocation: Sealed and not open to the public, East Talpiot, Jerusalem

Description: Rome's ancient state prison, the Carcer Tullianum: an upper chamber and a circular lower dungeon, the Tullianum, into which condemned prisoners — Jugurtha, Vercingetorix, the Catilinarian conspirators — were lowered to be strangled or starved. From the 8th century, Christian tradition held that Peter and Paul were imprisoned here before their martyrdoms, and a church grew over the cells. DOUBT STATED: there is no archaeological evidence and no early written account placing Peter or Paul in this prison; the Acts of Processus and Martinianus, the source of the tradition, is 6th century, and the well said to have sprung up for Peter's baptisms predates any apostolic connection. The prison is real; the apostolic connection is tradition only.
Interpretations: The building's history as Rome's prison is documented by Livy, Sallust, and Ammianus Marcellinus. The Peter-Paul tradition is medieval pilgrimage tradition, universally accepted from the 8th century but unsupported by any first- or second-century source. Placed in BORDERLINE because the biblical illumination depends entirely on that unproven tradition.
BiblicalSignificance: Peter and Paul were both martyred at Rome, and 2 Timothy 4 shows Paul imprisoned in Rome near the end, expecting death. The Mamertine shows what a Roman state prison meant — not a long-term jail but a death cell — and so illuminates the world of Paul's last imprisonment, without being shown to be its place.
ArtifactDate: Lower chamber (Tullianum) possibly 7th-6th century BC; upper chamber 2nd century BC; in use until the 4th century AD
CurrentLocation: In situ, Rome (beneath San Giuseppe dei Falegnami)
DiscoveryLocation: Foot of the Capitoline Hill, Roman Forum, Rome, Italy
